Labour Market Conditions and Further Education in the US since 2000

Group 37 – Introduction to Programming

Authors

Allotey Kelvin, Lloyd

Braun, Finn

Bruehwiler, Nils

Troillet, Cyril

Published

May 20, 2026

Research question

Do young Americans pursue further education in response to deteriorating labour market conditions in the US since 2000?

The intuition is simple. The opportunity cost of going back to school is the wage you would otherwise earn. When the labour market is weak, graduates have a more difficult time finding an entry-level job that suits their preferences. A weak labour market is often characterised by a high unemployment rate and/or low wage offers, among other factors. This circumstance leads many students to pursue further education in hopes of better times (staying in school longer has relatively lower opportunity costs). We test this hypothesis using master’s enrolment, the most common form of further education for students who already hold a bachelor’s degree.

Data

Our database holds nine series for the US since 2000:

  • Eight monthly series from FRED: unemployment rate (UNRATE), job-openings rate (JTSJOR), hires rate (JTSHIL), quits rate (JTSQUR), involuntary part-time work (LNS12032194), nonfarm payrolls (PAYEMS), the unemployment rate of bachelor’s-degree-and-above (LNS14027662), and the NBER recession indicator (USREC).
  • One annual series from NCES: total postbaccalaureate fall enrollment in US degree-granting institutions (MASTERS_ENROLLMENT), 2000-2022, from the Digest of Education Statistics, Table 303.80.

The data lives in a DuckDB star schema (see Figure 1) built once by data/build_fred.py. After the build, the database is the only data source for this brief, every figure and table comes from LabourMarketFramework in src/labour_market_framework.py.

A first look at the data

Table 1 summarises every series.

Two numbers from this table provide context for the rest of the analysis. UNRATE peaked at 14.8% in April 2020 and averaged 5.6% over the sample. Master’s enrollment grew from 2.16 million in 2000 to 3.21 million in 2022, a 47% rise in 22 years.

The labour market since 2000

Figure 2 plots job openings against unemployment, the Beveridge curve. A healthy market shows a downward slope: when unemployment falls, vacancies rise, and the points sit on one curve. Outward shifts indicate structural change.

Three patterns are visible. The 2001 and 2008-09 recessions show a move down and to the right (more unemployment, fewer openings). The April 2020 point sits at the extreme bottom right (as mentioned before: 14.8% unemployment, 3.4% openings). From 2021 onward the points lie above the historical curve at the same unemployment level: same unemployment, more openings than before.

A composite stress index

UNRATE captures one dimension of the labour market. To test our research question we want a broader approach, so we built our own labour-market stress index using the compute_stress_index method on our class.

How it is built. Four monthly FRED series enter the index by default: the quits rate (JTSQUR), the hires rate (JTSHIL), involuntary part-time work (LNS12032194) and nonfarm payrolls (PAYEMS). Each series is z-scored (mean 0, standard deviation 1) so that scales do not distort our results. Signs are then applied so higher values mean worse labour-market conditions: involuntary part-time work gets +1 (more part-timers stuck part-time = worse), quits, hires, and payrolls each get -1 (lower = worse). The four signed z-scores are averaged into one number per month.

Goal. Summarise the labour-market state in a single, comparable series so we can ask whether enrollment responds to the labour market measured as our index, rather than to one indicator like UNRATE alone.

Reading the index. Zero is roughly average for 2000-present. Positive readings mean conditions are worse than average, negative readings mean better.

The index lines up with the three recessions of our sample. It rises through the 2001 dot-com bust, peaks at the 2008-09 financial crisis, and spikes sharply in April 2020 before falling back again. Since 2022 a labour market is observed that, under historical comparison, is quite tight.

Enrollment and the stress index

Figure 4 puts the index next to the yearly growth of master’s enrollment. The left axis is the index (higher = worse), the right axis is enrollment growth.

The 2001 and 2008-09 recessions match our intuition closely. The index rises strongly during each recession, enrollment growth peaks roughly one year later, at 6.5% in 2002 and 4.1% in 2009. The one-year lag is explained by the length of the academic admission cycle: people who decide to go back to school during a downturn show up in enrollment data the next September.

The 2020 COVID-19 recession is the exception. The stress index peaked in April 2020, but enrollment growth in 2021 was only 2.3% - weaker than their responses to earlier recessions. A possible explanation could be that the pandemic e.g. disrupted admissions and on-campus life. These problems may have suppressed the effect that earlier recessions had on the master’s enrollment.

Discussion

The opportunity-cost intuition holds, with a 2020 exception. For the 2001 and 2008-09 recessions, master’s enrollment grew most when the broader labour-market was worst (Figure 4). The 2020 recession shows different results, that can be explained by e.g. closed campuses and disrupted admissions.

Limitations of our analysis. Master’s enrollment is annual and is stored at January-1 of each year, while the FRED series are monthly. We align the two using yearly growth, but the underlying admission decisions happen already earlier, not on the first of January. Also, master’s enrollment is measured in absolute figures, therefore, one has to take into account a growing US population (about 18% between 2000 and 2022) that partially explains growing master’s enrollment numbers as well. The NCES Digest has no 2023 figure yet, so the most recent enrollment observation is fall 2022. The involuntary-part-time series (LNS12032194) has one missing month at the very end of the sample, visible as a slightly shorter count in Table 1.

Conclusion

Master’s enrollment in the US has moved in line with labour-market stress for most of the period since 2000. The relationship is clearest for the 2001 and 2008-09 recessions, it does not hold for the 2020 COVID-19 episode, probably because other problems caused by the pandemic held against the usual effect. The reusable Python class LabourMarketFramework (see the User Guide) produced every figure and table in this brief, the same toolkit can be repointed at a different economy by swapping the DuckDB file.
